quick_summary: Simple harmonic motion is sinusoidal motion produced by a restoring force proportional to displacement. For a frictionless spring–mass system, Newton’s second law gives x″ = −(k/m)x, which leads to angular frequency ω₀ = √(k/m). Initial position and velocity determine the particular motion, while amplitude and phase describe its size and timing.

key_concepts.explanation: A physical quantity varies sinusoidally with time. Equivalent representations include y(t) = A sin(2πt/T) = A sin(2πft) = A sin(ω₀t).
The positive amplitude A is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. A sinusoidal displacement ranges between −A and +A.
The period T is the repetition time, so y(t + T) = y(t). Frequency is f = 1/T in hertz, and angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T = 2πf in radians per second.
Position x is measured from the spring’s equilibrium position. Positive x means extension, negative x means compression, and the initial displacement is x₀ = l₀ − l_eq.
The spring force is Fₓ = −kx. Its sign opposes displacement, so it acts toward equilibrium.
Newton’s second law gives m x″ = −kx, or x″ = −(k/m)x. Acceleration is proportional to negative displacement rather than being constant.
Substituting a sinusoidal trial solution into the oscillator equation requires ω₀² = k/m. Thus ω₀ = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k).
Because the oscillator equation is linear, sums of solutions remain solutions. Its general solution is x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
Evaluating position and velocity at t = 0 gives C = x₀ and D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. Therefore x(t) = x₀ cos(ω₀t) + (vₓ,₀/ω₀) sin(ω₀t).

The general solution can also be written x(t) = A cos(ω₀t + φ), with C = A cosφ, D = −A sinφ, and A = √(C² + D²). The phase must satisfy both coefficient relations; the inverse-tangent expression requires choosing the appropriate quadrant.
The phase is ω₀t + φ, and φ is the phase constant. Positive φ shifts the curve left and negative φ shifts it right. The maximum associated with phase zero occurs at t = −φ/ω₀.

learning_path.title: From Spring Force to Sinusoidal Motion
learning_path.reason: The lesson follows the source’s analytical development, beginning with periodic-motion notation and ending with amplitude and phase.

steps.title: Read a sinusoidal motion
steps.learning_goal: Distinguish amplitude, period, frequency, and angular frequency.
steps.explanation: In y(t) = A sin(ω₀t), A sets the displacement bounds and ω₀ sets the timing. One cycle takes T, with f = 1/T and ω₀ = 2π/T. Repetition means y(t + T) = y(t).
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the notation needed before analyzing the spring system.

steps.title: Turn a restoring force into an equation of motion
steps.learning_goal: Explain why the spring’s acceleration points toward equilibrium.
steps.explanation: Choose x = 0 at equilibrium. An extended spring has x > 0 but Fₓ < 0; a compressed spring has x < 0 but Fₓ > 0. Combining Fₓ = −kx with Newton’s second law gives x″ = −(k/m)x.
steps.connection_to_previous: The sinusoidal description is now connected to a physical force law.

steps.title: Verify a sinusoid and determine its frequency
steps.learning_goal: Derive ω₀ = √(k/m) by matching second derivatives.
steps.explanation: For x(t) = A cos(ω₀t), differentiating twice gives x″ = −ω₀²x. This matches the spring equation when ω₀² = k/m. Therefore T = 2π√(m/k): increasing mass lengthens the period, while increasing stiffness shortens it.
steps.connection_to_previous: The equation of motion tells us which derivative property a valid solution must have.

steps.title: Build a solution that can match different starts
steps.learning_goal: Understand why both sine and cosine terms are needed.
steps.explanation: A pure cosine starts at nonzero displacement with zero velocity. A pure sine starts at equilibrium and can have nonzero velocity. Since the equation is linear, their sum is also a solution: x(t) = C cos(ω₀t) + D sin(ω₀t).
steps.connection_to_previous: Knowing the frequency does not yet specify the initial position and velocity; two independent coefficients provide that flexibility.

steps.title: Use initial position and velocity
steps.learning_goal: Determine C and D from x₀ and vₓ,₀.
steps.explanation: Differentiate the general solution to obtain vₓ(t) = −ω₀C sin(ω₀t) + ω₀D cos(ω₀t). At t = 0, position gives C = x₀ and velocity gives D = vₓ,₀/ω₀. These select the particular motion for any initial position and velocity.
steps.connection_to_previous: The general solution’s free coefficients are now fixed by the physical starting conditions.

steps.title: Interpret amplitude and phase
steps.learning_goal: Connect initial conditions to oscillation size and horizontal shift.
steps.explanation: Rewrite the motion as A cos(ω₀t + φ). Matching coefficients gives C = A cosφ and D = −A sinφ, so A = √(x₀² + (vₓ,₀/ω₀)²). Use both coefficient signs to choose the correct phase quadrant. The horizontal shift is −φ/ω₀ = −φT/(2π): positive φ shifts left, while negative φ shifts right.
steps.connection_to_previous: The same initial-condition-specific solution is recast into quantities that are easy to recognize on a graph.

checkpoint_questions.question: A block is to the right of equilibrium, so x > 0. What does the spring model predict?

options.text: Acceleration is positive because displacement is positive.
Acceleration is negative and proportional to displacement magnitude.
Acceleration is zero unless the block is moving.
Acceleration is a constant negative value throughout the motion.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: The equation x″ = −(k/m)x gives negative acceleration for positive displacement. Its magnitude changes with displacement.

checkpoint_questions.question: If the mass is multiplied by four while the spring constant stays unchanged, what happens to the oscillation period?

options.text: The period is multiplied by four.
The period is divided by two.
The period is multiplied by two.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(m/k), multiplying m by four multiplies T by √4 = 2.

checkpoint_questions.question: A block starts at equilibrium with positive velocity. Which expression matches these initial conditions?
checkpoint_questions.explanation: With x₀ = 0, the cosine coefficient vanishes. The positive sine coefficient gives x(0) = 0 and x′(0) = vₓ,₀ > 0.
